items.abstract: <jats:p>We present evidence on how generative AI changes the work patterns of knowledge workers using data from a 6-month-long, cross-industry, randomized field experiment. Half of the 7,137 workers in the study received access to a generative AI tool integrated into the applications they already used for emails, document creation, and meetings. We find that access to the AI tool during the first year of its release primarily impacted behaviors that workers could change independently and not behaviors that require coordination to change: workers who used the tool in more than half of the sample weeks spent 3.6 fewer hours, or 31% less time on email each week (intent to treat estimate is 1.3 hours) and completed documents moderately faster, but did not significantly change time spent in meetings.<br><br>Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at <a href="http://www.nber.org/papers/&#119;33795" TARGET="_blank">www.nber.org</a>.<br></jats:p>

items.abstract: Most research on students’ GenAI use relies on frequency. Yet frequency captures exposure, not how students use GenAI. This study examined whether patterns of use are more informative for outcomes than frequency. Exploratory factor analysis of items developed inductively from pilot data identified two dimensions: evaluative integration (EI, use to support understanding), and low-verification uptake (LVU, shortcut use). Survey responses from 157 undergraduates were used to test associations with performance and indirect associations through academic self-efficacy (ASE), with frequency included for comparison. EI was positively associated with performance, whereas LVU was negatively associated with it. EI showed a significant indirect association through ASE and no remaining direct association; LVU showed both a significant indirect association and a remaining direct negative association. Frequency predicted neither performance nor ASE. In a separate model, frequency strengthened the positive association between EI and ASE, but the interaction was nonsignificant when the EI and LVU interactions were estimated jointly. No moderation was found for LVU. How students engage with GenAI may therefore be more informative for academic outcomes than frequency alone. The findings support further development of measures of student-GenAI interaction and testing of pedagogical approaches that promote evaluative integration.
title: Same Tool, Different Work: Patterns of Generative AI Use and Academic Outcomes

items.abstract: <jats:p>AI agents are increasingly central to information systems, yet conceptual understanding of their engineering patterns remains fragmented. But developing robust and ethically aligned AI agents requires clear conceptual patterns guiding engineering practices. This study performs a structured conceptual analysis using existing prompt engineering patterns aiming to conceptually map prompting patterns found in Generative AI to Agentic AI, focusing on fundamental agent characteristics and critical AI risks and opportunities. Results indicate significant conceptual gaps in addressing ethical decision-making and transparency while adequately covering autonomy and basic collaboration. The patterns also underpin in a very tangible manner, an increased abstraction in prompting in agentic systems aligning with larger agent autonomy. The paper contributes a conceptual taxonomy that highlights areas needing further conceptual and empirical exploration, recommending future studies for empirical validation. It is also of value to practitioners who are commonly well-experienced in Generative AI prompting and aim to transition towards instructing and defining agents.</jats:p>
title: Agentic AI Prompt Engineering: Advancing Generative AI Patterns Conceptually

items.description: Ishraque Hossain Chowdhury, PhD student, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, discusses generative AI in strategy work and firm performance, including the role of AI as a transformative resource, challenges organizations face when integrating AI, risks associated with AI strategic decision making, how human expertise can complement AI in achieving strategic objectives, and balancing technological capabilities with organizational goals.
title: Generative AI in Strategy Work and Firm Performance

items.abstract: <jats:p>Intelligence (AI) is a rapidly evolving subset of AI technologies that involves creating new content, such as text, images, and audio, using algorithms trained on large datasets. Well-known examples of generative AI technologies include Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT). These innovations are increasingly being integrated into various business applications, from automating content creation and enhancing customer interactions to driving product development and innovation. The importance of generative AI in a business context lies in its potential to augment human creativity, improve operational efficiency, and unlock new business opportunities, making it a critical tool for enterprises aiming to maintain a competitive edge in the digital age. Despite its transformational potential, the implementation of generative AI in businesses faces significant challenges. High implementation costs, the complexity of integrating AI systems into existing infrastructures, a shortage of skilled specialists, and ethical issues related to data privacy and AI-generated content are among the primary obstacles. Additionally, businesses often struggle to align AI initiatives with their strategic goals and ensure that AI outputs meet high standards of quality and compliance. These barriers complicate the large-scale and effective adoption of generative AI, limiting its potential to revolutionize business operations and innovation. The research encompasses a comprehensive review of existing literature, analysis of real-world cases, and synthesis of best practices in the strategic implementation of generative AI. It explores strategic models for the deployment of generative AI in enterprises, identifies key drivers and barriers to its adoption in business environments, and examines the strategic approaches businesses use to integrate generative AI into their operations. Insights and recommendations are provided for enterprises considering the adoption of generative AI technologies. The importance of the research lies in its potential to help businesses overcome implementation challenges and maximize the benefits of generative AI. Understanding strategic models and approaches to AI integration will enable businesses to better navigate the complexities of AI deployment, enhance their innovative capabilities, and ensure sustainable growth in an increasingly competitive market. The conclusions drawn from the research aim to bridge the gap between theoretical insights and practical applications of generative AI, providing a valuable resource for business leaders, technology strategists, and policymakers seeking to leverage AI for competitive advantage.</jats:p>
title: LEVERAGING GENERATIVE AI: STRATEGIC ADOPTION PATTERNS FOR ENTERPRISES
Generative AI at Work

items.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI assistants are increasingly used for software engineering tasks, but complex project work requires durable control over context, dependencies, permissions, process state, evidence and feedback across many sessions and artifacts. This paper introduces the AI Work Field Model, a design artifact for graph-governed trajectory control in generative AI-assisted development. The model represents AI-assisted work as movement through an external operational field composed of goals, system DNA, graph objects, typed relations, context profiles, lifecycle states, gates, evidence artifacts, feedback loops and cockpit metrics. The paper positions the model relative to design science, requirements traceability, RAG/GraphRAG, workflow management, LLM-based software engineering agents and human-in-the-loop AI. A public-safe synthetic method-inspection package demonstrates context projection, transition validation, evidence-boundary checking, cockpit summarization and expert-review-to-prevention mapping. The package produces illustrative synthetic results, including a mean context-unit reduction of 54.74% across four fixture tasks and successful validation of seven transition fixtures. The paper makes a bounded design-science claim: it defines and demonstrates the mechanics of an operational control model, while leaving independent empirical validation, production-quality claims and standardization to future work.</jats:p>
title: AI Work Field Model: Graph-Governed Trajectory Control for Generative AI-Assisted Development

items.abstract: <jats:p>New AI tools have the potential to change the way workers perform and learn, but little is known about their impacts on the job. In this paper, we study the staggered introduction of a generative AI-based conversational assistant using data from 5,179 customer support agents. Access to the tool increases productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 14% on average, including a 34% improvement for novice and low-skilled workers but with minimal impact on experienced and highly skilled workers. We provide suggestive evidence that the AI model disseminates the best practices of more able workers and helps newer workers move down the experience curve. In addition, we find that AI assistance improves customer sentiment, increases employee retention, and may lead to worker learning. Our results suggest that access to generative AI can increase productivity, with large heterogeneity in effects across workers.</jats:p>
title: Generative AI at Work

items.abstract: <jats:p>The sudden globalization of work, followed by the attendant decentralization of the working population, has spawned an unprecedented crisis in what has become known as Organizational Memory (OM). The aforementioned crisis has been followed by an unprecedented loss of knowledge exchange in tacit knowledge on one hand, and hubris in explicit knowledge organized in disconnected “silos” on another. Under these circumstances, this particular chapter sets out to assume that today and in tomorrow's future, there cannot possibly be any valid KM strategy capable of meeting, let alone succeeding in complying with, this new paradigm of distant work. Thus, we argue that it's time to propose Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models: sociotechnical innovations that propose and see within existing digital presence, in this case in our corporation's “corpus” dynamically coupled with Large Language Models (LLMs) to be henceforth and forevermore, sociotechnically speaking, “de rigueur” in thise new paradigm on distant work. They provide—in fact, literally “reanimate” existing passive repositories to be made query-capable as necessarily “digital synapses” to their existing analogs. Numerous existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation models, including “Retriever-Centric” and “Generator-Centric” models in particular, and even “Agentic” varieties in particular, shall be exhaustively described in this chapter.</jats:p>
title: Generative AI in Knowledge Management and Organizational Memory

items.abstract: <jats:p>This article presents preliminary investigations of generative AI technologies as tools for detecting dark patterns. This work is motivated by growing regulatory interest in dark patterns and deceptive online choice environments, and the need to development meaningful behavioural auditing tools as a response to these practices. We propose and offer initial explorations into three approaches to using generative AI to simulate the behaviour of online users with differing levels of digital skill. Our initial testing shows the ‘AI Vision’ approach to hold promise at present; the ‘Choose your own adventure’ approach to hold potential; and the ‘Decision Network’ approach to raise interesting technical challenges.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how firms create, process, and apply knowledge, yet little is known about the heterogeneity of its productivity effects across users. We report results from a randomized controlled experiment in which participants-analogs of early-career knowledge workers-were assigned to self-study a technical domain using either traditional resources or large-languagemodel (LLM) assistance. On average, GenAI access significantly increased task performance, but the distribution of gains was highly uneven. Improvements were not predicted by GPA or prior knowledge, but by AI Interaction Competence (AIC)-the ability to elicit, filter, and verify model outputs. High-AIC participants realized outsized gains; low-AIC participants saw limited or even negative marginal returns. A scaffolding intervention (conceptual maps) reduced outcome variance, indicating that standardized workflows can mitigate inequality in AI-mediated performance. We interpret these findings through the lens of human-AI complementarities: GenAI raises mean productivity while introducing a new axis of capability inequality. Managerially, firms should pair GenAI access with short AIC micro-training and simple standard operating procedures to capture value consistently and avoid uneven adoption outcomes.</jats:p>

<jats:p>This article examines the implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for work, job
<br>
transition and labour governance in Nigeria. It argues that the central challenge posed by GenAI
<br>
is not immediate mass unemployment, but the gradual reorganisation of tasks, managerial
<br>
authority, workplace surveillance and skill requirements in ways that may either strengthen or
<br>
weaken decent work. Drawing on the normative positions of the International Labour
<br>
Organization, UNESCO, the Council of Europe and the African Union, the article shows that
<br>
contemporary regulatory thinking increasingly treats AI as a governance issue requiring human
<br>
oversight, non-discrimination, transparency, accountability and support for worker transition. It
<br>
then analyses Nigeria’s legal and policy architecture, including the Constitution, the Labour Act,
<br>
the National Industrial Court’s labour jurisdiction, the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, the
<br>
National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025, the National Employment Policy 2025, the
<br>
National Digital Economy Policy and Strategy 2020–2030 and the Nigeria Startup Act 2022. The
<br>
article contends that while Nigeria possesses important normative and policy building blocks, its
<br>
framework remains fragmented and does not yet amount to a dedicated workplace AI
<br>
governance regime. It identifies key risks for Nigerian workers, including algorithmic bias,
<br>
intrusive monitoring, opaque decision-making, skill exclusion and the danger that AI may
<br>
modernise productivity while preserving informality. It concludes by proposing a practical
<br>
decent work agenda built around human review of significant AI-assisted employment decisions,
<br>
workplace transparency, data governance, social dialogue, structured reskilling and
<br>
sector-specific guidance. Ultimately, it argues that the future of work in Nigeria should be shaped
<br>
by law, policy and a deliberate commitment to decent work and social justice.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores the strategic potential and future trajectory of generative AI in energy systems. Unlike traditional predictive tools, generative models enable simulation of complex, uncertain, and novel scenarios, critical for addressing climate variability, behavioral dynamics, and infrastructure planning. They support climate-resilient modeling, personalized efficiency interventions, and stress-testing of energy systems under future conditions. However, their rise introduces pressing governance challenges around transparency, equity, and data use. The chapter concludes with strategic recommendations for researchers, utilities, and regulators to guide the responsible and impactful deployment of generative AI in energy transitions.</jats:p>

<jats:p>As AI companies perpetuate the rhetoric that generative AI enhances efficiency and automates away drudgery - and pursue ambitions to automate everything from customer service to medical diagnoses - it is critical that claims about the technology's capabilities do not go unchallenged. This primer integrates workers' current and material experiences into public discourse and questions promotional language about the magical, infallible, and seemingly inscrutable qualities of AI. It underscores that AI does not exist outside of industries' current economic conditions and their attendant inequalities and power dynamics. 

While media speculation has focused on whether and how AI can either "augment" work or drive mass unemployment, looking at the technology's impact on different industries reveals a more complicated story. Generative AI and Labor: Power, Hype, and Value at Work shows that understanding how AI will affect work requires examining how work is organized, how industries are structured, and whose and what work is valued.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This report examines the potential impact of Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems, such as ChatGPT, on the future of work and, by implication, on productivity. It argues that although Generative AI is powerful, it has significant limitations and risks that require humans to remain “in the loop” not only to prevent systems from going off the rails, but to capture value. Rather than taking a deterministic view that artificial intelligence (AI) will inevitably destroy jobs, the article suggests that an analysis should start with how firms can strategically deploy these tools to gain an advantage. It asks whether “augmentation” or “simplistic automation” lies ahead. Our objective is to move beyond hype and despair.<br><br>The existing digital infrastructure has enabled AI to be adopted quickly. However, projections based solely on automating existing tasks fail to capture the complex reorganizations that are likely to happen. Firms in sectors such as professional services, materials, and pharmaceuticals seem to have particular exposure to the use of Generative AI tools. Adaptations will vary across contexts and depend greatly on who controls the decisions about deployment. Maintaining the centrality of humans is likely to prove crucial—in training systems, curating data, and assessing outputs. One question is which business strategies and public<br>policies encourage that engagement and make it possible.<br><br>Although AI regulation debates matter, promoting social prosperity depends heavily on directly shaping the trajectory of the development and use of AI. This requires influencing the constraints and the incentives that firms face, as well as the strategic mindsets of decision makers. Which groups are engaged in the discussions and debates is of vital importance. The article recommends that, beyond the traditional policy proposals, an independent public-interest consultancy needs to be established in order to design creative business strategies that augment workers in a manner that will support, rather than hinder, social prosperity. Ultimately, avoiding a dystopian scenario might hinge on fostering new norms in which human capabilities remain essential.</jats:p>
title: Generative AI and the Future of Work: Augmentation or Automation?

items.abstract: <jats:p>We introduce a framework for understanding the impact of generative AI on human work, which we call the human–AI task tensor. A tensor is a structured framework that organizes tasks along multiple interdependent dimensions. Our human–AI task tensor introduces a systematic approach to studying how humans and AI interact to perform tasks, and has eight dimensions: task definition, AI integration, interaction modality, audit requirement, output definition, decision-making authority, AI structure, and human persona. After describing the eight dimensions of the tensor, we provide illustrative frameworks (derived from projections of the tensor) and a human–AI task canvas that provide analytical tractability and practical insight for organizational decision-making. We demonstrate how the human–AI task tensor can be used to organize emerging and future research on generative AI. We propose that the human–AI task tensor offers a starting point for understanding how work will be performed with the emergence of generative AI.</jats:p>

<jats:p><p>Lawyers routinely rely on generative AI platforms--both general-purpose tools such as Claude and ChatGPT and legally focused platforms such as Harvey, Legora, and CoCounsel--to analyze transactions, assess risk, draft documents, and structure legal advice for corporate clients. Currently, however, there is no agreement among federal courts on whether the attorney-client privilege or work product doctrine protects these communications. Four landmark 2026 decisions frame the debate. United States v. Heppner (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 17, 2026) held that documents a criminal defendant generated using a consumer AI platform were not privileged or protected as work product. Warner v. Gilbarco, Inc. (E.D. Mich. Feb. 10, 2026) reached the opposite conclusion, holding that AI-assisted litigation materials constitute protected work product and that treating AI tools as third parties for waiver purposes would "nullify work-product protection in nearly every modern drafting environment." Morgan v. V2X, Inc. (D. Colo. Mar. 30, 2026) substantially extended Warner, analogizing AI to email, phones, and smart devices, and introduced AI-specific protective order language. And the Sixth Circuit in United States v. Farris (Apr. 3, 2026) issued ethical guidance emphasizing safeguarding privilege when attorneys use AI. The critical unresolved question is how courts will treat attorney-directed use of closed, proprietary AI systems that contractually prohibit vendor access to client inputs.</p>
<p>This Article makes three main arguments. First, the work product doctrine, although more easily applied to AI, is insufficient because it applies only in anticipation of litigation. Much of the most consequential AI-assisted legal work--M&amp;A due diligence, regulatory compliance, contract drafting--occurs in transactional contexts where work product offers no protection. This limitation makes essential the privilege recommendations this Article proposes.</p>
<p>Second, it argues that waiver analysis related to use of AI should be similar to that applied to other third-party vendors like e-discovery vendors, or contract analytics tools used by lawyers. As long as there is a reasonable expectation of confidentiality, Federal courts have never held that uploading privileged materials to contract analytics software, e-discovery platforms, or legal research tools constitutes a third-party disclosure that waives privilege or work product protection.</p>
<p>Third, this Article argues that AI platforms should be analyzed under the same doctrine applied to human third-party consultants. AI platforms are functionally the most capable consultants in the history of the legal profession. The question is not whether they are "real" third parties in a philosophical sense, but whether they perform functions that, when performed by humans, courts have protected or declined to protect. However, applying that framework reveals that the emerging doctrine is at once potentially too narrow and too broad. Under the narrowest interpretation, use of AI would be categorically excluded from the privilege framework even when the substantive conditions for privilege—attorney direction, legal purpose, maintained confidentiality— are fully satisfied. Under the broadest application, courts might protect all inputs to, outputs from, and communications with a closed AI platform. This is because when AI is involved, the “legal purpose” inquiry becomes so easy to satisfy on the attorney's side and extremely hard to successfully challenge on the opponent's side, particularly in circuits applying the significant purpose test. This creates a de facto zone of secrecy even though the doctrine formally requires legal purpose, a problem amplified by the unresolved circuit split between the primary purpose and significant purpose tests left intact by the Supreme Court's dismissal of In re Grand Jury as improvidently granted.</p>
<p>This Article proposes analysis under a single, uniform agency-based standard requiring a strong nexus between the AI's function and the legal advice ultimately provided, assessed through four factors: (1) who directed the AI use; (2) the nature of the platform--enterprise and closed, or consumer and open; (3) what is being sought to be protected--an output, input, prompt, or communication exchange; and (4) the purpose of the use, specifically whether providing legal advice was a primary or significant purpose. Unlike a categorical rule, this multi-factored nexus test embraces the essential role AI plays in the provision of high-quality legal advice while preventing corporations from using AI-laundered communications as a discovery shield.</p></jats:p>

items.description: Artificial intelligence, in particular Large Language Models (LLMs), are commonly considered being a path-breaking innovation. While possible applications and rising research questions are manifold, one straightforward question of very general interest is whether LLMs can support humans in fulfilling job-related tasks, hereby improving the quality and quantity of the output. In this study, we will focus on the impact of LLM and LLM training on teachers in adult education.
